expectations.text: Claude identifies the $32 as a LATE estimate — the treatment effect for compliers (users who adopted because of the push notification) — not the ATE for the full user population or the policy-relevant effect for a forced rollout
expectations.evidence: The response opens with 'The LATE estimated from the encouragement design applies only to compliers — the specific subset of users who adopted the feature because they received the notification.' It also states '$32 estimate represents the average revenue uplift only for the compliers' and explicitly distinguishes LATE from ATE: 'LATE ≠ ATE. The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) for the full population could be higher or lower than $32.'

expectations.text: Claude explains why LATE ≠ ATE for forced adoption: forced rollout affects never-takers (who actively declined the notification) whose response to forced adoption is unknown and likely much smaller or negative — the LATE tells us nothing about how they would respond
expectations.evidence: The 'Why the Force-Rollout Expectation Is Wrong' section explains that force-rollout reaches never-takers (~82% of users who 'received a push notification and still didn't adopt'), that 'Never-takers are, by revealed preference, unresponsive to the notification,' and that the effect for never-takers is 'Not identified — this is exactly what we need.' The response also notes possible negative effects: 'Forced feature activation on unwilling users can cause frustration, support ticket volume, or increased churn — potentially negative revenue effects.'

expectations.text: Claude does NOT confirm that $32/user is the right planning figure for a forced adoption rollout
expectations.evidence: The Short Answer opens with 'No, $32 per user is not the right expectation for a force-rollout.' Practical Recommendation #1 states: 'Do not use $32 as the forecast for the force-rollout. It is the wrong estimand for the wrong population.' The Summary reinforces: 'Projecting $32/user onto that population conflates the LATE with the ATE.'

expectations.text: Claude recommends a forced-adoption experiment (random assignment to feature enabled vs. disabled regardless of opt-in) to estimate the ATE before committing to the forced rollout decision
expectations.evidence: The 'What Estimate Would Be Appropriate?' section recommends 'randomly force-enable the feature for a subset of non-adopters and measure the revenue outcome.' Practical Recommendation #2 specifies: 'Run a holdout experiment before full rollout. Force-enable the premium feature for a random 10–20% of non-adopters and measure 6-month revenue vs. a control group of non-adopters. This gives the direct causal estimate needed.'
